replace: distinguishing such errors from a lack of jurisdiction that is open to collateral review
reason: Fauntleroy addressed legal error versus jurisdiction. Its holding does not exclude other recognition defenses or permit relitigation of jurisdiction already fully and fairly adjudicated.

find: Here, State A has two potent \textit{Fauntleroy}-compatible defenses that flip the outcome: (1) \textit{lack of personal jurisdiction} in State B (which Holmes expressly preserved as a valid collateral attack, 210 U.S. at 237, and which Y did not waive by defaulting), and (2) the \textit{penal-judgment exception} (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/146/657/}{\textit{Huntington v. Attrill}, 146 U.S. 657 (1892)}), arguing that a state-brought punitive fine---unlike Fauntleroy's private contract/arbitration recovery---is a penal obligation that sister states need not execute.
replace: State A may refuse enforcement if the fine punishes a public wrong rather than compensating a private injury, under the penal-judgment exception in \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/146/657/}{\textit{Huntington v. Attrill}, 146 U.S. 657 (1892)}. Because Y defaulted, Y may also contest State B's personal jurisdiction, though deliberately mailing regulated goods into State B may supply sufficient forum contacts.
reason: Default leaves personal jurisdiction open to challenge, but never physically entering the forum does not itself establish the defense. Huntington classifies penalties by their purpose.
